extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and policymakers interested in automotive recalls and safety incidents
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate the facts, causes, legal outcomes, and safety implications of a major automotive recall (General Motors ignition switch defects). Suitable for readers seeking an encyclopedic account of the recall, investigation, compensation, and regulatory response.

rubrics_metrics.name: GM ignition switch torque specification
rubrics_metrics.description: GM's own standards required the ignition switch torque to be between 10 N·cm and 20 N·cm (Newton centimeters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If torque was less than 10 N·cm the switch was 'a force so little that made it prone to changes in modes which could potentially shut off the engine.' This torque spec was used by GM engineers as a pass/fail criterion for switch acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignition switch vibration-resistance requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The switch was required to 'withstand exposure to a vibration environment without damage or loss of function.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GM's specification meant the switch should not change modes during 'extreme moments of vibrations, or even with the presence of heavy objects on a keychain.' Failure to meet this requirement could cause the switch to move from Run to Accessory, shutting off engine power to steering, brakes, and airbags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory absence of ignition switch torque/vibration standards
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no specified torque or vibration standards imposed on a vehicle's ignition switch by the NHTSA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This regulatory gap meant manufacturers set their own criteria; absence of federal specs is noted as a contributing context to the defect not being regulated to a specific numerical standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design function that removes airbag power in Off/Accessory
rubrics_metrics.description: The ignition switch was designed to remove power from the vehicle's airbags when in the Off or Accessory mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the switch could move from Run into Off/Accessory, that design characteristic made a mode change a direct safety hazard: airbags would no longer be powered and could fail to deploy in a crash.

rubrics_metrics.name: GM's criteria for counting recall-linked deaths
rubrics_metrics.description: GM counted only 'incidents resulting in head-on collisions in which the airbags did not deploy' when linking deaths to the ignition switch defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This narrow counting rule excluded cases where ignition failure led to secondary crash sequences (e.g., spinning out and hitting another vehicle or environmental hazards) or where only some occupants' deaths were attributed to airbag non-deployment. The policy influenced the company's publicly reported death totals and was a point of dispute with investigators and media analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation program categories and eligibility process (Feinberg plan and GM fund)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kenneth Feinberg's compensation fund accepted applications within a defined window (August 1, 2014 until end of year) and administered awards; GM's compensation program referenced Category One and Category Two injuries and awarded compensation accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feinberg had 'the last word' on compensation amounts; as implemented the GM compensation fund 'offered compensation for 124 deaths' but rejected a large fraction of claims (more than 90% rejected by the compensation fund, per reporting). The article notes differences in counting/eligibility and that many claims were excluded or denied, affecting the final compensated totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deferred Prosecution Agreement elements for corporate disclosure failures
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of the Deferred Prosecution Agreement, GM admitted that it 'failed to disclose a deadly safety defect to its U.S. regulator' and 'forfeited $900 million to the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The DPA required an admission of failure to disclose and substantial forfeiture; such agreements can be used as a remedial/prosecutorial outcome when a corporation's non-disclosure of safety defects is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory expectation vs. manufacturer claim on airbag deployment duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal safety regulators testified they had expected airbags in the defective cars 'to be able to deploy for 60 seconds after the engine stalled,' while General Motors later told the Associated Press that they actually can only do so for 150 milliseconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discrepancy was used in Congressional/agency questioning to evaluate GM's statements about vehicle safety and the adequacy of their information provided to regulators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties for failing to cooperate or delaying a recall
rubrics_metrics.description: NHTSA fined GM $28,000 for not supplying requested information by a deadline and charged $7,000 for each day afterward GM did not provide the information; separately, GM agreed to pay the Department of Transportation the maximum fine of $35 million for delaying the recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies impose monetary penalties tied to statutory/regulatory deadlines and cooperation requirements; these fines quantify regulatory enforcement for failures to timely disclose or act on safety defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of timely availability of repair parts and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: GM said parts needed to repair the faulty ignition switches were expected to become available on April 7, 2014, but dealerships reported not receiving parts that day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely distribution of replacement parts and repair procedures is an implicit requirement of an effective recall; delays hinder remediation and are a metric for assessing the recall's implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate disclosure and ethical obligations (internal communication to management and compliance laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article states GM lawyers and engineers 'were evidently aware of the defect since 2005 and failed to communicate this issue to the upper management,' and that by not disclosing such pertinent information they 'violated clearly defined ethical obligations under state rules and federal law such as the Sarbanes–Oxley Act.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies are expected to escalate known safety defects through internal channels and to regulators; failure to do so can constitute violations of corporate governance and disclosure laws and is used as an evaluative standard in legal and reputational assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineering decision-making tradeoffs (cost/time vs. safety fixes)
rubrics_metrics.description: GM engineers 'decided not to fix this issue because it was costly and time-consuming.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights a criterion used in internal decision-making—whether the cost and time required to implement a fix justify action—which is an evaluative axis for how organizations prioritize safety vs. resource expenditures. The article presents this as a factor contributing to delayed remediation.
